title: Review: Dynamic equilibrium and Kc expressions; Kc calculations and Q; Le Chatelier and industrial compromise
source: Questions copied unchanged from the mission-lesson scripts for AP Chemistry (status of the source: mission-lesson scripts of Oct-Nov 2026 (reviewed by AI reviewers; not signed off by a person)). Terms and clues: EQ01#t3 term and clue written for the game; EQ02#t4 term and clue written for the game; EQ01#t1 term and clue written for the game; EQ02#t1 term and clue written for the game. Questions: EQ01#N.3b, EQ02#N.14, EQ03#N.2, EQ01#N.13, EQ02#N.5, EQ03#N.12b, EQ01#N.10b, EQ02#N.3b, EQ03#N.10, EQ01#N.6, EQ02#N.10, EQ03#N.14b. The matching task revisits terms from the worlds it reviews, in a new mix. Some questions repeat from the worlds it reviews.

assemble.prompt: Match each term to its definition.

items.label: Closed system
items.clue: A set-up in which nothing enters or leaves.

items.label: Equilibrium constant
items.clue: The value K, which only a change in temperature can alter.

items.label: Reversible reaction
items.clue: A chemical change that can go both ways, shown with the symbol ⇌.

items.label: Le Chatelier's principle
items.clue: When a system at equilibrium is disturbed, it shifts so as to partly oppose the change.

questions.stem: A sealed flask at constant temperature contains a mixture of brown NO₂(g) and colorless N₂O₄(g), which interconvert by the reaction N₂O₄(g) ⇌ 2 NO₂(g). The intensity of the brown color has not changed for an hour. Which of the following best explains why the color stays the same?

options.text: NO₂ is formed and used up at equal rates, so the amount of NO₂ stays constant.
NO₂ has stopped forming and stopped reacting, so the amount of NO₂ stays constant.
NO₂ and N₂O₄ are now present in equal amounts, so the color has stopped changing.
The two rate constants have now become equal, so the color has stopped changing.

questions.stem: Methanol is made from CO(g) + 2H₂(g) ⇌ CH₃OH(g). The forward reaction is exothermic. Plants run it at high pressure. Why does raising the pressure, by reducing the volume, increase the equilibrium yield of methanol?

options.text: K increases at high pressure, so more methanol is present at equilibrium.
The forward reaction is exothermic, so high pressure pushes the position right.
The position shifts right: the right side has fewer moles of gas.
More frequent collisions at high pressure speed up the forward reaction only.

questions.explanation: 3 mol of gas on the left, 1 on the right. Raising the pressure favours the side with fewer gas molecules, which partly opposes the change.

questions.stem: For the hypothetical reaction A(g) + B(g) ⇌ C(g), Kc = 4.0 at a certain temperature. At one moment, a reaction mixture at this temperature has Q_c = 25. Which statement correctly describes the mixture at that moment?

options.text: The forward reaction is faster than the reverse reaction, so [C] rises
The forward and reverse reactions are equally fast, so [C] stays the same
Only the reverse reaction occurs, and it continues until Q_c equals Kc
The reverse reaction is faster than the forward reaction, so [C] decreases

questions.explanation: Q_c = 25 > Kc = 4.0, so [C]/([A][B]) is too large. Net consumption of C and formation of A and B until Q_c = Kc.

questions.stem: A mixture of hydrogen and chlorine can be kept in the dark for days with no visible change. Yet for H₂(g) + Cl₂(g) ⇌ 2HCl(g), K ≈ 2 × 10³³ at 298 K. What do these facts tell you?

options.text: At equilibrium it would be mostly H₂ and Cl₂, because no HCl forms in the dark.
It is already at equilibrium, because nothing changes while it is in the dark.
At equilibrium it would be almost all HCl; in the dark it reacts extremely slowly.
It must react quickly in the dark, because a very large K means a fast reaction.

questions.explanation: K ≫ 1, so the equilibrium lies far to the right. K tells you how far, not how fast: in the dark the reaction is too slow to see.

questions.stem: CH₄(g) + H₂O(g) ⇌ CO(g) + 3H₂(g). The pressure is increased, by reducing the volume, at constant temperature. What happens?

options.text: The position shifts right, giving more H₂; K is unchanged.
The position shifts left, giving less H₂; K decreases.
There is no shift, because every species is a gas.
The position shifts left, giving less H₂; K is unchanged.

questions.explanation: 2 mol of gas on the left, 4 on the right. Higher pressure favours the side with fewer moles of gas, the left. Temperature is constant, so K is unchanged.

questions.stem: For the hypothetical reaction X₂(g) ⇌ 2 X(g), Kc = 3.6 × 10⁻⁶ at a certain temperature. A rigid container at this temperature is filled with X₂ to an initial concentration of 0.10 M, with no X present. What is the equilibrium concentration of X?
questions.explanation: [X₂] ≈ 0.10 M (Kc is very small), so [X]² = (3.6 × 10⁻⁶)(0.10) = 3.6 × 10⁻⁷ and [X] = 6.0 × 10⁻⁴ M. Only 0.3% of the X₂ dissociates.

questions.stem: A student plans to mix equal volumes of 0.20 M X(aq) and 0.10 M Y(aq) at 25°C, where they react according to the hypothetical equation X(aq) + Y(aq) ⇌ Z(aq), Kc = 5 × 10¹¹ at 25°C. After the mixture reaches equilibrium, the student will measure the concentrations of the three species. Which prediction about the equilibrium [Y] is correct?

options.text: [Y] will be exactly zero, because all of the Y is used up
[Y] will remain near 0.050 M, because Y barely reacts with X
[Y] will be very small but not zero, because Kc is very large
[Y] will be 0.025 M, because [Y] and [Z] become equal at equilibrium

questions.explanation: After mixing, [X] = 0.10 M and [Y] = 0.050 M. The reaction goes almost to completion, so [Z] ≈ 0.050 M, [X] ≈ 0.050 M and [Y] = [Z]/(Kc[X]) ≈ 2 × 10⁻¹² M: tiny, but not zero.

questions.stem: The hypothetical reaction D(g) + E(g) ⇌ G(g) is at equilibrium in a rigid container with [D] = 0.20 M. More D(g) is then injected, which raises [D] to 0.50 M at the moment of injection. Which statement describes [D] once equilibrium is re-established at the same temperature?

options.text: It stays at 0.50 M, its value just after the injection
It settles at a value between 0.20 M and 0.50 M
It rises to some value that is greater than 0.50 M
It returns to 0.20 M, its value before the injection

questions.explanation: Q < K, so net forward reaction uses up some D. The stress is only partly counteracted: if [D] fell all the way to 0.20 M, with less E and more G than before, Q would exceed K.

questions.stem: At a certain temperature, reaction 1, 2 SO₂(g) + O₂(g) ⇌ 2 SO₃(g), has equilibrium constant K₁, and reaction 2, 2 NO(g) + O₂(g) ⇌ 2 NO₂(g), has equilibrium constant K₂. Which expression gives the equilibrium constant at the same temperature for the reaction SO₂(g) + NO₂(g) ⇌ SO₃(g) + NO(g)?

options.text: K₁/K₂
√(K₁/K₂)
√(K₁ × K₂)
K₁ × K₂

questions.explanation: Half of reaction 1 plus half of the reverse of reaction 2 (½ O₂ cancels). Halving takes square roots, reversing inverts K₂, adding multiplies: √K₁ × √(1/K₂).

questions.stem: Which is the equilibrium constant expression for 4NH₃(g) + 5O₂(g) ⇌ 4NO(g) + 6H₂O(g)?

options.text: Kc = [NO]⁴[H₂O]⁶ / ([NH₃]⁴[O₂]⁵)
Kc = [NO]⁴ / ([NH₃]⁴[O₂]⁵)
Kc = [NH₃]⁴[O₂]⁵ / ([NO]⁴[H₂O]⁶)

questions.explanation: Products over reactants, each raised to the power of its coefficient. All four species are gases, so H₂O(g) is included.

questions.stem: A test tube holds orange potassium dichromate(VI) solution: 2CrO₄²⁻(aq) + 2H⁺(aq) ⇌ Cr₂O₇²⁻(aq) + H₂O(l). Sodium hydroxide solution is added drop by drop. What is seen, and why?

options.text: It turns yellow, because OH⁻ removes H⁺ and the position shifts left.
There is no change, because OH⁻ does not appear in the equation.
It turns a deeper orange, because the added base speeds up the forward reaction.
It turns yellow, because the alkali lowers the value of K.

questions.explanation: OH⁻ reacts with H⁺ to form water. Losing H⁺ shifts the position left, towards yellow chromate(VI).

questions.stem: H₂(g) + I₂(g) ⇌ 2 HI(g), K = 54 at 700 K. A sealed flask at 700 K holds [H₂] = 0.20 M, [I₂] = 0.050 M and [HI] = 0.80 M. It looks unchanging. Calculate Q. Will it react, and which way?

options.text: Q = 0.016, less than K: net forward reaction; [HI] rises.
Q = 64, greater than K: net forward reaction; [HI] rises.
You can't tell until the flask has been left to settle.
Q = 64, greater than K: net reverse reaction; [HI] falls.

questions.explanation: Q = (0.80)²/((0.20)(0.050)) = 0.64/0.010 = 64 > 54. Too much HI, so it decomposes until Q = 54; more violet I₂ forms.
